gloss: Either Light was subsequent to the Deity, as being the first thing created by Him, or Light existed from Eternity equally with Him. It has been well said that there is something peculiarly personal and sensitive in Milton’s references to light.
dost thou prefer to be called? A classicism; cf. Lat. *audire*, as in Horace’s *seu Jane libentius audis* (*Sat.* II. vi. 20).

lemma: Through utter and through middle darkness
gloss: *utter* darkness, of Hell, as always in M.: *middle* darkness, of Chaos. M. means that in II. 629–1055 he described the flight of Satan through Hell, and thence upward through Chaos towards Heaven. *utter*, outer.
*quenched*, the metaphor of putting out a light. *orbs*, used of the eye-balls; cf. *oculorum orbes* in *Aeneid* XII. 670.

His love of literature, in particular classical poetry, has not failed. He is still devoted to those ancient poets inspired by the Muses who haunted the “hill” of Helicon, with its “clear springs” Aganippe and Hippocrene, and Parnassus with the famed Castalian fountain.

But his love of the classics is exceeded by his love of Scripture. “Sion hill” and “Siloa’s brook” and the brook Kidron: these scenes and the literature associated with them—the Psalms of David and the works of the singers of Israel—are dearest to him.

Milton was best inspired at night or daybreak. Newton in his *Life of M.* says that the poet’s widow, “being asked who the Muse was, replied it was God’s grace, and the Holy Spirit that visited him nightly.”

*Thamyris*, according to Homer, *Iliad* II. 595–600, a Thracian bard, who, for boasting that he could surpass the Muses in song, was deprived of his sight. *Mæonides*, i.e. Homer; called Mæonides, either as a son of Mæon, or as a native of Mæonia, the ancient name of Lydia.

*Tiresias*, the blind soothsayer of Thebes, famous through the *Œdipus Rex* of Sophocles. *Phineus*, another blind prophet, king of Salmydessus in Thrace; best known in connection with the Harpies. In his second Letter to Leonard Philaras (Sept. 28, 1654) M. compares himself with Phineus.
*numbers*, verse. *the wakeful bird*, the nightingale, Milton’s favourite bird, if we may judge by his many references to it.

the sight of him. An allusion to the *Visio Beatifica*. Cf. M. in *The Christian Doctrine*, I. 33, “Perfect glorification consists in eternal life and perfect happiness, arising chiefly from the divine vision.”

i.e. the side nearest to the Empyrean. The realm of Night (personified) lies in Chaos, between Hell and the Empyrean. Into the upper regions of this realm penetrates the light reflected from the battlements of the Empyrean, and forms a kind of half-light—what M. calls a “dun” atmosphere, i.e. brownish, dusky.

Viewed from outside, this Universe appeared to be a solid, spherical mass of land, without sky (the sky which we see being supposed to be inside the “first convex” or outer crust). *Uncertain*, it being uncertain. Chaos, in which it hung, was a mixture of land and sea.

That the rebellious angels, like Adam and Eve, had free will, to obey or disobey, is emphasised in V. 525–43 and elsewhere. Cf. *The Christian Doctrine*, I. 3, “in assigning the gift of free will, God suffered both men and angels to stand or fall at their own uncontrolled choice.”

“When God gave him reason, he gave him freedom to choose, for reason is but choosing,” *Areopagitica*. Reason is speculative: will, practical—in fact, the power of putting reason into action. It is by reason that we choose the right course, by will that we take it.

cf. 1 Timothy v. 21, “the elect angels,” which M. explains in *The Christian Doctrine*, I. 9, to mean “beloved, or excellent.” In *P. L.* this Scriptural word marks off the good angels from the revolted.

referring to the use in the New Testament of ‘Word’ (Vulgate *verbum*), as a title of the Son. *effectual might*, i.e. power by whom the will of the Father was effected, e.g. in the creation of the World.
the doctrine of predestination here alluded to is discussed by M. at some length in *The Christian Doctrine*, I. 4.
*affecting*, seeking to win; Lat. *affectare*, ‘to aim at.’ The Serpent tempts Eve with the promise of godhead, IX. 708.

utterly doomed. The words have practically the same meaning: *sacred* = Lat. *sacer*, ‘dedicated to a deity for destruction’; *devote* = Lat. *devotus*, ‘set apart as by a vow (*votum*)’ with the same object.

All the angels of Heaven shrink from the task of saving man, just as all the fallen angels—their leader excepted—shrank from undertaking the expedition to ruin man. The Saviour himself must achieve the one work, as the Tempter himself the other (Newton).
unanticipated (i.e. by prayer); grace comes before man has prayed for her. *prevent* = Lat. *prævenire*, ‘to come before.’
hurl down. M. uses *ruin* = Lat. *ruina* in its literal sense ‘fall.’ Thus in I. 46 he speaks of the “ruin” of the angels from heaven.

referring to the doctrine of imputed righteousness which M. deals with in the chapter “Of Justification,” *The Christian Doctrine*, I. 22. He writes, “As therefore our sins are imputed to Christ, so the merits or righteousness of Christ are imputed to us through faith.”
all titles of the three Hierarchies of Heavenly beings. *Princedoms* = ‘Principalities.’
an absolute construction. The Angels are a “Chorus” such as M. contemplated for his drama on the subject of *Paradise Lost* (Dunster).

the unfading flower. Perhaps the idea of the flower being transferred was suggested by the Rabbinical doctrine that after the Fall of Man “the Garden, with its contents, was removed to Heaven” (Keightley).

cf. Isaiah vi. 2, “Above it stood the seraphims: each one had six wings; with twain he covered his face.” M. chooses the Seraphim as being the most lustrous of the Heavenly Orders; yet even they cannot bear the extreme radiance.

cf. *The Christian Doctrine*, I. 5, “certain it is that the Son existed in the beginning, under the name of the logos or Word, and was the first of the whole creation.” That chapter (“Of the Son of God”) reveals Milton’s Arianism very clearly.

the Primum Mobile or tenth sphere, formed of solid matter, and serving as the outer shell of the World, and so dividing from Chaos the nine other spheres (= “luminous inferior orbs”) which are inside.

The elaborate form of the simile is very characteristic. Like Vergil, M. often works a simile out in all its bearings. Here the comparison is very apposite; the vulture = Satan; the flocks = mankind, Satan’s prey; the barren plains = the “continent” where he alighted.

The germ of the whole idea lies in Ariosto’s *Orlando Furioso*, canto 34. M. says that there is (as people thought) a Paradise of Fools, the rubbish-heap of the Universe: only it is situated, not in the moon, but on this outside of the globe where Satan is walking.

he means the “mighty men … men of renown,” who were born of the “sons of God” and “the daughters of men” (Gen. vi. 4). In XI. 621–25 M. identifies the “sons of God” with the pious descendants of Seth; in V. 447 he regards them as angels.

a Greek philosopher of Agrigentum in Sicily. “He threw himself into the flames of Mount Ætna, that by his sudden disappearance he might be believed to be a god; but the volcano threw up one of his sandals and thus revealed the manner of his death” (*Classical Dictionary*).
a philosopher of Ambracia in Epirus; according to the legend, he drowned himself after reading Plato’s description of Elysium in the *Phædo*, in order that he might exchange this life for a better.

*white*, the Carmelites, so called after Mt Carmel; *black*, the Dominicans, an order of preaching friars founded in 1215 by St Dominic; *grey*, the Franciscans, founded in 1209 by St Francis of Assisi. From their respective garbs the three orders were known in England as the White Friars, the Black Friars, and the Grey Friars.

i.e. that sphere which with its balance determines the amount of the swaying motion (“trepidation”) so much talked about. *talked*, talked of; this contemptuous word rather implies that M. did not believe in the theory. *that first moved*, the Primum Mobile, or tenth sphere.
intended as a sneer (cf. the depreciatory word “wicket”) at the Roman Catholic doctrine of ‘the power of the keys’; cf. Mat. xvi. 19, “And I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven.”

All terms specially associated with the Roman Catholic Church. *reliques*, relics, like the remains of the bodies or clothes of Saints and Martyrs. *beads*, of the rosary. *indulgences*, such as the Roman Church grants. *dispenses*, dispensations. *bulls*, papal edicts; so called from the round leaden seal, *bulla*.
Gen. xxviii. 11–17. Probably Milton’s notion of a stair connecting the Universe with Heaven was suggested by Jacob’s dream.

i.e. the second passage mentioned in 531. The Old Testament often speaks of angels visiting the Earth, and here we are told that there were two aerial paths for their descent, one leading straight down from Heaven on to Mount Sion, the other extending over the whole Promised Land.
i.e. “from Dan even to Beer-sheba” = from N. to S. of Canaan. *Paneas*, the later Greek name of Dan, a little S. of Mount Hermon, at the foot of which the Jordan has its chief source.

Was M. recalling to memory one of the Italian cities visited on that tour in 1638–39 to which his thoughts reverted so gladly? Perhaps Florence on which he had looked down from Fiesole; or, yet more likely, Rome. The epithet “glistering” suggests an Italian scene.

Aries, the Ram—exactly opposite in the Zodiac (in the west) to Libra, the Balance (in the east). M. says that the constellation Andromeda is borne by Aries because it lies above Aries in the sky. *the horizon*, i.e. of this Earth.

those Islands of the Blessed, to which, according to an early Greek belief, favoured mortals passed without dying. Later these *Fortunatæ Insulæ* came to be identified with islands off the west coast of Africa (probably the Canaries).

Newton explains: up or down, north or south; *by center or eccentric*, towards the centre, or from the centre; *longitude*, east or west. Other editors note that M. leaves it undetermined whether the sun or the Earth is the centre of the Universe, i.e. whether the Copernican or Ptolemaic astronomy is right.
probably he is thinking of Galileo, who in 1609 constructed a telescope (“optic tube”) by which the spots on the solar disc were perceptible. *tube*, the common 17th century word for the telescope.
“the philosopher’s stone.” *Philosophers*, alchemists, who tried to compose a stone which would transmute other metals into gold.

the prophetic old man of the sea. To escape prophesying, he would transform himself into “various shapes”; but when he was firmly seized he would return to “his native form” and foretell the future. Milton uses this legend to illustrate the processes of alchemists.

“Where Satan was,—i.e. on the Sun itself,—all was sunshine without visible shadow, just as, on Earth, at the equator at noon, the Sun’s beams striking vertically downwards cause opaque objects to have no slanting shadow round them” (Masson).

dress, Lat. *habitus*; probably in apposition to *wings*, as Milton’s angels are always “feathered,” not clothed (Newton). *succinct*, literally ‘girt up’; hence ‘ready, prepared.’ *decent*, graceful, becoming.

in the chapter of *The Christian Doctrine* on angels, M. says, “Seven of these, in particular, are described as traversing the earth in the execution of their ministry.” Of these Uriel was one. That he was “regent of the sun” was a tradition, due probably to his name which signifies ‘the fire of God.’

A fine and just allegory that a wise man may be deceived through the very greatness of his nature: for he is filled with high thoughts, not mean suspicions: which makes him trust his fellow-men, and credit them with being as honest and true as himself.

Uriel must have been among the angels who accompanied Messiah when he went forth to create the World, VII. 192–215. The lines reveal the influence of Plato’s account of the creation (*Timæus*) and of Ovid’s description of Chaos (*Metamorphoses* I. 5 et seq.).

M. refers to Aristotle’s conception of a fifth element called “ether,” and he introduces the two main points of Aristotle’s theory: (1) that “the ether fills the celestial spaces, and of it the spheres and stars are made”; (2) that “the nature of the ether adapts it especially for circular motion.”

referring to the three phases of the moon—crescent, full and waning. But there is also an allusion to Lat. *triformis* as an epithet of the moon indicating her threefold capacity as Luna, Diana and Hecate.
‘the snowy range’; a mountain of Armenia, part of the Taurus range—on the borders of Assyria.
